item.research_question: Can machine learning models accurately predict the elastic constants (C11, C12, C44) of refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) using a dataset generated from density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and which model performs best?
item.material_system: Refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) with BCC structures containing Cr, Hf, Ta, Ti, Mo, Nb, W, Re, Zr, and V; specific compositions include TiZrVNbMo, TiZrNbMo, TiZrVNb, MoNbTiZr, MoNbTiVZr, NbTiVZr, and NbTaTiV
item.processing_route: Database generation via CALPHAD (Thermo-calc-2019) to identify stable BCC phases, followed by DFT calculations using VASP with GGA-PBE, 500 eV cutoff, and SQS models (8 to 125 atoms); Machine Learning training using Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR), and XGBoost with 90% training/10% testing split and GridSearchCV hyperparameter tuning
item.test_conditions: DFT calculations performed at 0 K; ML models validated against 4 unseen experimental and simulation datasets; Performance metrics included R-squared, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)
key_findings: The Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR) model achieved the highest prediction accuracy with R-squared values of 0.97 for C11, 0.803 for C12, and 0.787 for C44 on the testing dataset.
The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for the GBR model was below 5 GPa for training data and less than 11 GPa for testing data.
Valence Electron Concentration (VEC) and Melting Temperature (MT) were identified as the top two most influential descriptors for predicting elastic constants.
Higher VEC, MT, and Geometric Parameter (GP) values, combined with lower omega (Ω) values, correlate with higher elastic constants in refractory alloys.
The GBR model predictions for TiZrVNbMo, TiZrNbMo, and TiZrVNb showed good agreement with SQS model calculations, with average error bars smaller than the deviations.
The predicted C11 elastic constant for NbTaTiV matched the experimental value reported by Lee's study very well.
The study utilized a dataset of 370 RCCAs generated from DFT calculations to train the models.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that VEC and MT are critical because VEC influences lattice distortion and phase stability (e.g., BCC stability when VEC < 6.87), while higher melting temperatures favor higher elastic constants; the GBR model optimizes bias by iteratively training trees to learn from previous mistakes, avoiding early paralysis and overfitting.
item.limitations: The dataset size of 370 instances is relatively small; the ML models do not consider complex phenomena such as lattice defects, dislocations, grain boundaries, slip planes, and plastic deformation; the DFT calculations were performed at 0 K while experiments were at 300 K, causing temperature-related discrepancies; the model cannot predict elastic constants at varying temperatures.
item.future_work: Future work should focus on creating an ML model that can predict elastic constants at varying temperatures; more high-throughput experimental methods are needed to confirm findings for specific alloys; experimental measurement of lattice distortion is required to gain further knowledge about element contributions; more powerful models should be developed to account for complex phenomena like defects and plastic deformation.
quotes: The GBR model was found to be most promising in predicting the elastic constant of RCCAs among the three ML models.
The R2 value for all models ranges from 0.76–0.97 for the training and testing datasets.

The GBR model is not capable of predicting the elastic constants of RHEAs at different temperatures and therefore future work should be focused on creating an ML model that can predict the elastic constants at varying temperatures.
